notes:
I've put together notes on most verses. There are some gaps. I couldn't reach any Catholic or Orthodox commentary (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org); the only Catholic material I found was Douay-Rheims wording on Bible Hub. I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on verses 1–22. Enduring Word's prosperity material covers verses 25–43, which is outside your passage. The full Enduring Word chapter and Matthew Henry are at https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/ and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Ellicott says Rachel's barrenness was a real grief, but her words sound petulan[t] and peevish[]… in strong contrast with Hannah's patient suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-1.htm
- Benson and Matthew Henry make the same comparison: Rachel envied, Hannah wept, and the reader is told to copy Hannah, not Rachel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-1.htm
- Clarke calls the speech most reprehensible. To him it shows envy and a complete lack of dependence on God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/genesis-30.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew for "envied" is connected with the redness of an angry face. It reads "I die" as "I am a dead woman" for shame at being barren. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-1.htm
- Utley (bible.org) also says "jealous" literally means "red in the face". https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-30
- Gill thinks Rachel can't have believed Jacob could give her children himself. Perhaps she meant he should pray for her, as Isaac prayed for Rebekah, or find some other way for her to have children. He also says "I die" was not a threat of suicide. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-1.htm
- Matthew Henry mentions a minority view that she was threatening to kill herself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm
- JFB links the urgent longing for children among Hebrew women to the hope of giving birth to the promised seed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-1.htm
- The irony: Guzik notes that both halves came true. She had children and she died as a result. (Genesis 35.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/ Coffman calls it Rachel's "rash prayer." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-1.html

**v. 2**
- Matthew Henry calls Jacob's reply grave and pious. The Aramaic paraphrase he quotes has Jacob ask whether she ought not to seek sons from the Lord. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm
- Keil and Delitzsch say Jacob was right that he was not God. But he lacked a power he could have had, the power of prayer, in firm reliance upon the promise of the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-1.htm
- Guzik says Jacob saw God's hand in the matter but put it to Rachel so bluntly even though he stated it to Rachel cruelly. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Gen/Gen_30.cfm

**v. 3**
- Guzik compares this to Sarah giving Hagar to Abraham in Genesis 16. He reads "on my knees" (the older wording of v. 3) as an ancient custom of surrogate adoption. Some take it as a symbolic gesture; others take it literally. He says we can't be sure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- Matthew Henry suggests Rachel preferred her maid's children to her sister's because she could rule over them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm

**v. 4**
- Guzik says "as a wife" does not mean a real marriage. It means Jacob did with Bilhah what a man should do only with his wife. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: Dan means "judgment." Out of envy, Rachel saw a child born through human scheming as her victory and vindication. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- Keil and Delitzsch read it more kindly. God gave her justice, heard her prayer and took away the shame of childlessness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-8.htm
- Barnes says God had judged her for being self-satisfied, then heard her when she asked humbly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-8.htm

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik finds the boast odd, since Leah had four sons to Rachel's two. Perhaps Rachel meant that Leah had stopped having children. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- Matthew Henry says the names make it seem as if all Jacob's sons must be born men of contention. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm
- The Geneva Bible's note sees human arrogance in Rachel condemning her sister after receiving God's gift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-8.htm

**vv. 9–11**
- Guzik: Leah copied Rachel's surrogate method. Gad means "troop" or "good fortune," and the children had become pawns. Leah also seems to have lost the peace she showed when she named Judah ("praise"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- Keil and Delitzsch say Leah noticed quickly that she had stopped having children because her first four births came so close together. They argue the births are grouped by mother, not strictly in time order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-22.htm
- Kelly notes that Leah does not mention God's name at all when naming Gad and Asher. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-8.html

**vv. 12–13**
- Guzik: Asher means "happy." Leah cared more about the status the child gave her than about the child himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: "wheat harvest" dates the scene to about early May, and "mandrakes" literally means "love-apples." The Cambridge Bible says the plant was thought to work as a love-charm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-14.htm
- Reuben's age: Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary say four or five; Ellicott says fifteen to twenty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-14.htm
- Gill thinks they may simply have been pretty flowers of the kind children pick, and says it is hard to know what they were. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-14.htm
- Utley says Rachel hoped they would help her conceive — again the covenant family trying to help God. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-30
- Calvin admits the story looks trivial, yet it contains a useful instruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-14.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: Leah insists Jacob is *her* husband, whom Rachel has taken away. He uses this to support God's plan of one man and one woman, and notes that Leviticus 18:18 later forbids marrying two sisters. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- Matthew Henry infers that Jacob spent more time with Rachel. He says Rachel's strong feelings led her into the bargain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm

**vv. 16–17**
- Guzik: we don't know whether mandrakes worked biologically or as a placebo. Whatever means God allows, the real cause was His sovereign will ("God listened to Leah"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- A Bible Hub study article says putting the two side by side shows that God, not the plant, opens the womb. Scripture records the trade without recommending it. https://biblehub.com/q/Mandrakes_role_in_Genesis_30_14.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik: Issachar means "reward." Leah took the boy as God's reward for "generously" giving her maid to Jacob. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/

**vv. 19–20**
- Guzik: Zebulun means "dwelling." Leah, still hurting, hoped six sons would finally win her husband's heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/

**v. 21**
- Guzik sees nothing obviously symbolic in Dinah's name. He says nobody "won" the competition. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/
- JFB says the bare announcement shows the lower value placed on a daughter at the time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-22.htm

**v. 22**
- Calvin: God never forgets. Scripture speaks of His "memory" from the effect His acts have on us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-22.html
- Ellicott: years of barrenness had probably humbled Rachel. She stopped trusting in "love-apples" and looked to God. https://biblehub.com/genesis/30-22.htm
- Barnes: God acted at the best time, after teaching her dependence and patience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-22.html
- Matthew Henry: God may refuse a mercy we want too much, then give it after long waiting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_030.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary compares Genesis 8:1 and 1 Samuel 1:19. It notes that God treated Rachel as He had treated Leah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-22.htm
- Constable says the gifts came in spite of the parents' behaviour, not because of it. He notes that "God remembered Noah" and "God remembered Rachel" both sit at the turning point of their stories. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-22.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

The commentators I read largely agree; I found no real dispute between denominations. The church-tradition labels below are mine; the pages themselves don't use them.
- **v. 8, whether Rachel was praying:** Barnes reads "wrestlings of God" as both sisters wrestling with God in prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-8.htm Keil and Delitzsch (Lutheran) quote Hengstenberg ("fightings for God and His mercy") and Delitzsch. They reject Knobel's "a conflict in the cause of God" and the plain "very great wrestlings." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-8.htm Calvin (Reformed) lists the "twisting/joining" readings but prefers the simple "divine or excellent wrestlings." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-8.html Clarke (Methodist) prefers "twist/entwine." He cites Parkhurst's idea that Rachel's family was now intertwined with her sister's, giving her a chance of producing the promised Seed. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/genesis/30-8.html
- **v. 22, grace and prayer:** this is a difference of emphasis, not a dispute. Ligonier (Reformed) says Moses mentions God remembering Rachel before her prayer to show us that divine grace initiates all of our blessings. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/god-remembers-rachel Clarke stresses her response instead: her prayer and faith obtained what her impatience and unbelief had prevented. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-22.html

## 3. Other views
- **v. 14 (NET Bible note):** mandrakes were popularly thought to be an aphrodisiac in that culture. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=gen&chapter=30&verse=14
- **v. 8 (older translations):** Douay-Rheims (Catholic) has "God hath compared me with my sister," and the Greek Septuagint has "God has helped me." https://biblehub.com/genesis/30-8.htm
- **Source criticism (vv. 22–24):** the Pulpit Commentary mentions scholars who see the switch from "God" to "Jehovah" in the next verses as a trace of a separate source (Tuch, Bleek). It rejects this, and so do Keil and Delitzsch. They explain the switch by Rachel's growing faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-22.htm
